TERMS &CONDITIONS

Human behaviour
at tourist places

A study of how visitors behave in tourist spaces—and how place, information, infrastructure and social dynamics influence what people notice and do.

01

Context / The study

Every place has its own rules.
Not all of them are written.

Tourist spaces are shaped by more than their architecture or attractions. Visitors respond to information, other people, social expectations and the way a place is organised.

This study investigated human behavioural patterns across four tourist contexts in Gujarat. Through contextual observation, behavioural coding and cross-site analysis, it examined how visitors interacted with their surroundings and with information presented in those spaces.

The aim was to identify recurring patterns and deviations, understand the context influencing them, and explore opportunities to improve visitor engagement with information without disrupting the experience of the place.

“What people notice—and what they overlook—is part of the experience design.”

*Behaviour count and wording to be verified against the final research dataset.

02

Intent / Method

From looking
to understanding.

The study moved from contextual observation to behavioural interpretation and design exploration.

Research objectives

  1. Understand visitor behaviour across different tourist contexts.
  2. Identify recurring patterns and deviations in visitor actions.
  3. Compare behaviour across four distinct sites.
  4. Explore contextual factors influencing visitor behaviour.
  5. Develop design directions that could improve information engagement.

Research process

Contextual observationField notes and visitor actions
Behavioural codingTagging and classification
Cross-site analysisCompare patterns between places
Causal mappingExplore possible relationships
Deviant behaviour mappingIdentify differences and clusters
Design simulationsTranslate findings into directions
03

Fieldwork / 376 observations

Small actions.
Recurring patterns.

The observations were tagged across engagement, movement, social context, authority, group behaviour, risk, technology and gendered roles.

Authority & intended behaviour

The presence of authority can shape how visitors interpret expectations and behave within a space.

Herd-driven navigation

Visitor movement may follow surrounding crowds and collective flow rather than signage alone.

Spectacle dominates attention

Visually intense attractions can compete with nearby informational content for attention.

Information ignorance

Informational and educational content may be overlooked when visitors prefer quicker visual scanning.

Social hierarchies

Group roles and social structures can influence movement, interaction and decision-making.

Experience as performance

Photography and social media can shape where people pause and how spaces are used.

Risk normalisation

Repeated exposure to a setting may make some risks feel familiar or less urgent.

Spatial engagement

Movement and attention may vary across visitor groups, attractions and environmental conditions.

Short attention & turnover

Visitors may spend brief periods at individual points, moving on before exploring information in depth.

Synthesis / Deviant behaviour mapping

Look for relationships,
not isolated moments.

Mapping brought observations together to explore how engagement, risk and photo documentation appeared across sites.

The synthesis connected recurring behavioural themes to the four locations. Rather than treating each action as an isolated incident, the mapping helped identify areas for further design exploration.

Behaviour clusters

Three ways information
gets experienced.

The research poster groups observations into three broad clusters. The figures below are reproduced from the supplied poster and should retain their original definitions when presented.

A

Information ignorance

Information may be present but remain unnoticed or unengaged with.

47%noticing

B

Information engagement

Information receives attention and may prompt a more deliberate response.

06

Design simulations

What if information
worked differently?

Three exploratory directions translated the research into possible interventions for tourist environments.

Simulation 01

Visual data intervention

Make information more visually accessible through clear graphics, hierarchy and contextual cues.

Simulation 02

Curiosity-driven interaction

Use short storytelling facts or curiosity cues to invite visitors to pause and explore information.

Simulation 03

Auditory storytelling

Explore how audio cues and short narratives might complement visual information in a place.

The graphics above are illustrative representations of the three directions, not photographs of built or tested interventions.

07

Key insights

Attention is only
the beginning.

The supplied research poster lists eight insights around visibility, curiosity, sensory stimulation, information delivery and behavioural context.

01

Information competes with leisure priorities in recreational spaces.

02

Visibility alone does not guarantee engagement.

03

Curiosity can act as a behavioural trigger for information engagement.

04

Sensory stimulation can increase cognitive attention.

05

Information engagement depends on delivery, not just availability.

06

Engagement is a highly situational behaviour.

07

Herd behaviour can be a strong stimulus in the context of the trigger.

08

Cognitive overload can reduce grasping and retention in dense information environments.

08

Design implications

Design for the way
people actually move.

The project suggests opportunities to connect information with the visitor's environment, attention and motivations.

01

Strategic visibility

Position information near natural lines of sight, pauses and transitions instead of treating signage as an isolated object.

02

Audience-centred information

Consider visitor types, time constraints and attention spans when deciding how information is structured and presented.

03

Multi-sensory approaches

Explore visual, auditory and environmental cues that may support attention and engagement.

04

Contextual storytelling

Integrate narratives into the spatial experience so information feels connected to the place rather than separate from it.

05

Spatial storytelling

Use the visitor's route, transitions and points of interest to organise information as part of the journey.

06

Design opportunity

Redesign information systems to improve consumption, integrate documentation with information, and explore behaviour-guided spatial design.
